1. The Android system

Carefully review chapters 1 and 2 (in your textbook) and lecture slides on eLC
cards.backText:
Study the Android introduction and development tools in Lecture 1: IntroToMobileDevelopment and Lecture 2: AndroidStudioSetup. For this deck, the lecture slides supply the material; no textbook content has been added.

  • Versions: Lecture 1, pp. 25–27.
  • Licensing: Lecture 1, pp. 24 and 28.
  • Architecture: Lecture 1, pp. 34–41.
  • Google service APIs: Lecture 1, p. 42.
  • Android Studio, Gradle, emulator: Lecture 2, pp. 3, 18, 20–23.

Slides: 1, pp. 24–42; 2, pp. 3, 18, 20–23. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
1. The Android system

Be able to state a few of the most recent versions of the Android system
cards.backText:
The newest numbered versions listed in the professor’s version table are Android 15, Android 16, and Android 17. The table also lists Android 12, 13, and 14.

The informal dessert names shown for 15, 16, and 17 are Vanilla Ice Cream, Baklava, and CinnamonBun, respectively. These answers follow the lecture table rather than an independently updated release list.

Slides: 1, pp. 25–27. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
1. The Android system

Be able to describe Android system licensing
cards.backText:
The slides describe Android as free and open source: developers and device manufacturers pay no royalties or license fees. Its licensing is split across components:

  • Linux/kernel side: GNU GPL version 2 (GPLv2), described as strong copyleft.
  • Android framework: Apache Software License / Apache 2. The slides say framework developers do not have to contribute their improvements back to the open-source community.

Be able to associate GPLv2 → Linux and Apache 2 → framework; do not describe every Android component as having the same license.

Slides: 1, pp. 14, 24, 28. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
1. The Android system

Understand the basic Android architecture
cards.backText:
Know the layers in the architecture diagram, from the user-facing top down:

  • System apps: applications using the platform services.
  • Java API framework: reusable UI and system APIs, including Views, Activity Manager, resource management, notifications, and content providers.
  • Native C/C++ libraries and Android Runtime (ART): libraries provide shared platform capabilities; ART executes application code.
  • Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL): interfaces for hardware such as audio, Bluetooth, camera, and sensors.
  • Linux kernel: security and permissions, memory management, processes/threads, networking, and device drivers.

The slides state that each app runs in its own VM in a separate process. Dalvik was used before Android 5.0; Android 5.0 replaced it with ART. The lecture describes ART’s ahead-of-time conversion of app bytecode to machine code at installation. Remember the separate app processes and sandboxing as part of isolation/security.

Slides: 1, pp. 34–37, 39–41. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
1. The Android system

Be able to name 3 common Google APIs for Google services
cards.backText:
Three examples directly listed in the slides are Maps, Places, and Google Sign-In.

Other listed examples include Firebase, in-app billing/subscriptions, Google Cloud Messaging, mobile app analytics, Play Game Services, and AdMob. If asked to name three, Maps, Places, and Google Sign-In are sufficient.

Slides: 1, p. 42; 2, p. 19. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
1. The Android system

Be able to describe (in general) Android Studio and its basic components (IDE, Java compiler, Gradle, the Emulator) and their purposes
cards.backText:
• Android Studio / IDE: an integrated development environment based on IntelliJ IDEA. It brings together editing, project organization, layout tools, building, running, and debugging.
  • Gradle: the build automation system. It coordinates the project build and its libraries/plugins; build configuration and synchronization are part of the Studio workflow.
  • Emulator: runs a virtual Android device on the computer so you can run, test, and debug an app in different device configurations. The slides say it is not a substitute for testing on a real device.
  • Java tooling: the setup slides identify the bundled JDK/JBR.

Keep the roles distinct: the IDE is your workspace, the compiler translates source, Gradle coordinates the build, and the emulator runs the app for testing.

Supplemental explanation: The slides name the Java tooling but do not explain the compiler’s role directly. A Java compiler translates .java source into .class bytecode; Android’s build tools then prepare that code for Android execution. The compiler is different from ART on the device.

Slides: 2, pp. 3, 6, 18, 20–23; 5, pp. 11–13, 43–55. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
2. Event-driven systems

Carefully review lecture slides on eLC (Java GUI)
cards.backText:
Use Lecture 4: JavaGUI-EventDriven, especially pp. 2–13 for the core model and pp. 22–29 for handler implementations. Study the relationship event source → dispatcher → registered handler, and contrast that with procedure calls.

Slides: 4, pp. 2–13, 22–29. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
2. Event-driven systems

Be able to describe a procedure-driven system
cards.backText:
A procedure-driven system follows a flow of procedure/method calls. The caller invokes a procedure, transfers control to it, and waits while it executes; control returns to the caller when the procedure finishes.

The program’s procedural flow determines what runs next. For example, a main method calls a calculation method and then continues with the next statement after that method returns.

Slides: 4, p. 4. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
2. Event-driven systems

Be able to describe an event driven system
cards.backText:
An event-driven system responds to events as they occur. It registers handlers/listeners for events, and an event dispatcher/event loop invokes the appropriate handler when an event arrives.

For a GUI, the next action depends on the event received—such as a button click or key press. A handler can still call ordinary methods; the event determines when the handler begins.

Slides: 4, pp. 2–3, 5–6, 9–13. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
2. Event-driven systems

Be able to describe events – give examples
cards.backText:
An event is an occurrence the system can detect and respond to. The slides give examples including keyboard input, mouse actions/button clicks, arrival of a message, and timer events.

A GUI control acts as an event source: clicking a button generates an event, which is delivered to its registered handler. Events therefore do not have to come from a user; a timer or arriving message can also trigger a response.

Slides: 4, pp. 2, 8–10. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
2. Event-driven systems

Be able to describe event handlers (also referred to as callbacks or listeners)
cards.backText:
An event handler is code that responds to a particular event. The lecture also calls these callbacks or listeners. A handler must be registered with the event source; the system invokes it when the corresponding event occurs.

The JavaFX slides show a separate EventHandler class, a method reference, and a lambda. A compact JavaFX registration looks like:

button.setOnAction(event -> {
    System.out.println("Button clicked");
});

An Android click-listener example, using the pattern in the Android slides:

Button button = findViewById(R.id.pushButton);
button.setOnClickListener(view -> {
    count++;
    countText.setText(Integer.toString(count));
});

The registration runs while setting up the UI; the listener body runs later when the button is clicked.

Slides: 4, pp. 9–10, 22–29; 6, pp. 50–51. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
2. Event-driven systems

Be able to describe an event dispatcher
cards.backText:
The event dispatcher runs the event-processing loop. It accepts events and routes each event to the registered handler/listener for that event source.

The slides distinguish system-provided dispatching from application-provided handlers. In the Android discussion, the Looper participates in this dispatching/event-loop mechanism. The application supplies the response code; it does not manually call every click handler whenever a user clicks.

Slides: 4, pp. 3, 5–6, 11–13. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
3. Android application components

Carefully review chapter 4 and lecture slides on eLC
cards.backText:
Study Lecture 8: ApplicationComponents for lifecycle, saved state, and Intents; use Lecture 6: SecondApp-LayoutEditor for Activity examples and lifecycle sequences. Manifest examples appear in Lectures 5, 8, and 10. The textbook reading is represented here by the supplied lecture material.

Slides: 6, pp. 3–9, 65–72; 8, pp. 4–69; 10, pp. 41–42. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
3. Android application components

Describe an activity and give some examples
cards.backText:
An Activity represents a screen/window through which the user interacts with an Android app. Its UI can contain multiple Views/widgets, and the Activity manages its lifecycle and interactions.

The game example in the slides uses separate Activities for a splash screen, main menu, game play, high scores, and help. An app may have several Activities; later fragment examples also show multiple UI pieces hosted inside one Activity.

Slides: 6, pp. 3–6; 12, pp. 3–10. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
3. Android application components

Describe what is the activity stack (back stack)
cards.backText:
The activity stack / back stack records Activities in last-in, first-out order. The foreground Activity is at the top.

  • Starting a new Activity places it above the previous Activity; the previous one becomes paused and may become stopped when covered.
  • When the top Activity finishes, it is removed from the stack and the previous Activity can resume.
  • This stack explains returning to an earlier Activity with Back.

Example: Menu → Game → Help. With Help on top, finishing Help returns to Game; finishing Game returns to Menu.

Slides: 6, pp. 7, 64; 8, p. 4. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
3. Android application components

Describe the activity life cycle – be familiar with all of the main lifecycle callbacks
cards.backText:
Know all seven main Activity callbacks:

  • onCreate(Bundle): initialize the Activity and create its UI; restore saved state when available.
  • onStart(): the Activity becomes visible.
  • onResume(): the Activity is in the foreground and ready for interaction; resume work/acquire needed resources.
  • onPause(): the Activity is losing foreground interaction, possibly while still visible; prepare to stop, pause animations/playback, and release resources as described in the lecture.
  • onStop(): the Activity is no longer visible.
  • onRestart(): called when returning from the stopped state, before onStart().
  • onDestroy(): final cleanup when the Activity is destroyed; the slides warn that a process killed for low resources may not get this callback.

Common sequences:
Initial launch: onCreate → onStart → onResume.
Stopped and returning: onRestart → onStart → onResume.
Brief interruption: onPause → onResume.
Normally finishing: onPause → onStop → onDestroy.

@Override
protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState);
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main);
}

Slides: 8, pp. 5–29; 6, pp. 65–72. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
3. Android application components

Describe why is saving application’s state necessary, considering device orientation changes or an application being killed due to low resources
cards.backText:
An orientation change can destroy and recreate the Activity. Android may also kill a background app’s process when resources are low. Values stored only in fields—such as a count or selected list index—can be lost when new instances are created.

Save the UI state in the Bundle passed to onSaveInstanceState, and restore it in onCreate (or onRestoreInstanceState). A Bundle holds key–value pairs. Do not rely on onDestroy to save important data; it may not run when the process is killed.

private int selectedIndex = 0;

@Override
protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState);
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main);
    if (savedInstanceState != null) {
        selectedIndex = savedInstanceState.getInt("selectedIndex", 0);
    }
    // Use selectedIndex to restore the selected content.
}

@Override
protected void onSaveInstanceState(Bundle outState) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState);
    outState.putInt("selectedIndex", selectedIndex);
}

The fragments slides’ AndroidVersionsFragments example uses a selected list index to show the appropriate details after rotation. The Activity slides also distinguish saved UI state from application data that needs persistent storage.

Slides: 8, pp. 27, 36–43; 12, pp. 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
3. Android application components

Describe the purpose of an Intent and know how to start a new activity
cards.backText:
An Intent is an asynchronous message describing an action to perform. The slides show Intents used with Activities, services, and broadcast receivers. An explicit Intent identifies the target component; Intents can also carry extra key–value data.

Inside an Activity, start another Activity with an explicit Intent:

Intent intent = new Intent(this, DetailsActivity.class);
intent.putExtra("selectedIndex", selectedIndex);
startActivity(intent);

The target Activity can read the extra:

Bundle extras = getIntent().getExtras();
if (extras != null) {
    int selectedIndex = extras.getInt("selectedIndex");
}

The target Activity must be declared in the app’s manifest. The slides also show action/data Intents, such as viewing a URI.

Slides: 8, pp. 53–64. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
3. Android application components

Describe the general purpose of the AndroidManifest.xml file
cards.backText:
AndroidManifest.xml describes the app to Android. The examples declare the application and its Activities, identify the launcher Activity with an intent filter, request permissions, and specify parent Activity relationships for Up navigation.

<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
    <application android:label="@string/app_name">
        <activity android:name=".DetailsActivity"
            android:parentActivityName=".MainActivity" />
        <activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:exported="true">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>
    </application>
</manifest>

This example assumes the named Activities and string resource exist in the project.

Slides: 5, pp. 18, 21; 8, pp. 8, 55–69; 10, pp. 41–42; 7, pp. 106–111. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Carefully review lecture slides on eLC (XML)
cards.backText:
Use Lecture 10: XML: data/markup pp. 2–12; elements/attributes pp. 15–20; namespaces pp. 25–27 and 43–45; schema pp. 28–30; Android uses pp. 41–48. Practice reading a layout and distinguishing tags, attributes, and namespace prefixes.

Slides: 10, pp. 2–48. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Be able to the role of XML in computing (in general)
cards.backText:
XML (Extensible Markup Language) is a text-based markup format for representing structured, often hierarchical data. Tags annotate the data so its structure and meaning can be understood and exchanged between systems.

The lecture presents XML as a data/document representation and interchange mechanism, rather than a programming language. The tag names describe the data; XML itself does not supply the behavior of an Android button or Activity.

Slides: 10, pp. 3–12. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Understand XML tags and elements
cards.backText:
A tag marks an element’s beginning or end; an element is the complete unit, including its tags and content. Elements can contain text, child elements, or both. An empty element can use a self-closing tag.

<student>
    <name>Daniel</name>
    <course code="Mobile" />
</student>
  • <name> is a start tag; </name> is its end tag.
  • <name>Daniel</name> is the whole name element.
  • <course code="Mobile" /> is an empty element with an attribute.
  • Child elements are nested within their parent; closing tags must match the nesting.

Slides: 10, pp. 9–16. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Describe the purpose of XML attributes
cards.backText:
XML attributes supply additional information about an element. They appear as name–value pairs in the element’s start tag (or empty-element tag), with the value quoted.

<Button
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Submit" />

Here android:text="Submit" sets the Button’s label, and the width/height attributes set its sizing. The Button is the element; text, layout_width, and layout_height are attributes. Attributes configure the element without becoming separate child elements.

Slides: 10, pp. 17–20, 47–48. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Understand the purpose of XML schema
cards.backText:
An XML schema defines the structure and rules allowed in an XML document, so the document can be checked for validity.

  • Which elements and attributes are allowed.
  • How elements relate, including their order and number of occurrences.
  • Data types and restrictions on values.
  • Default values when specified.

The slides introduce DTDs and then XML Schema / XSD. An XML document can have correctly nested tags but still violate its schema—for example, by containing a disallowed child element or an invalid value type.

Slides: 10, pp. 21–24, 28–30, 34–35. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Understand the need for XML namespaces and convenience of namespace prefixes
cards.backText:
Namespaces prevent naming conflicts when a document uses names from different vocabularies. A namespace URI identifies the vocabulary; a prefix is a short local name bound to that URI.

<LinearLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical" />

The declaration binds android to the namespace URI. The prefix lets you write android:orientation instead of repeatedly writing a long namespace identifier. A prefix is an alias; the associated URI determines the namespace. The lecture’s other examples use separate prefixes to distinguish identically named elements.

Slides: 10, pp. 25–27, 43–45. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Be able to name one of the commonly used Android XML namespace prefixes
cards.backText:
A commonly used Android XML namespace prefix is android:

xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"

Examples are android:id and android:text. The slides also show app for application/support-library attributes (such as ConstraintLayout constraints) and tools for development-tool attributes.

Slides: 10, pp. 43–45. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
4. XML

Name 2 ways in which XML is used in Android app development
cards.backText:
• App manifest: AndroidManifest.xml describes the app, its components, permissions, and related configuration.
  • UI layouts: XML layout resources describe Views/widgets, their properties, and their arrangement. An Activity loads a layout with setContentView(R.layout.layout_name).

These are the two uses explicitly identified by the XML lecture.

Slides: 10, pp. 41–42; 6, pp. 16–18. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Carefully review chapter 7 and lecture slides on eLC
cards.backText:
Study Lecture 6: SecondApp-LayoutEditor for Views, IDs, setters, and units; Lecture 7: ExploringBuildingBlocks for individual widgets; and Lecture 11: IntroductionToLayouts for padding and adapter examples.

ViewPager is only mentioned and R.java is used without a direct explanation. Their cards explicitly identify the supplemental explanation. “EditView” in the attributes bullet is treated as EditText, the widget named elsewhere in the review and slides.

Slides: 6, pp. 11–18, 46–61; 7, pp. 6–111; 11, pp. 19–21, 70–87. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Describe a View in Android (in general)
cards.backText:
An Android View is a rectangular building block of the UI. It occupies an area of the screen and provides display and/or interaction behavior.

The android.view.View class is the base class for UI widgets. Examples include TextView, EditText, Button, and ImageView. ViewGroup is a special View that contains other Views, and layout classes generally extend ViewGroup.

Slides: 6, pp. 11–14, 19; 11, pp. 9, 15. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Understand the need for a View’s identifier in XML
cards.backText:
A View’s identifier lets application code retrieve that View and lets other Views refer to it in a layout—for example, when defining constraints.

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/countText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="0" />
TextView countText = findViewById(R.id.countText);
countText.setText("1");

@+id/countText declares the ID; R.id.countText refers to it from Java. Call findViewById after loading the layout containing the View. A View you need to manipulate should have an ID; IDs also distinguish Views in saved UI state and layout references shown in the slides.

Slides: 6, pp. 16–18, 46–48; 7, p. 6; 11, pp. 93–107. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Describe the purpose of View padding
cards.backText:
Padding is space inside a View’s bounds, between its content and its edges. It gives text/images breathing room within that View.

android:padding="16dp"
android:paddingStart="8dp"
android:paddingTop="12dp"

Use the all-sides padding attribute or side-specific padding attributes. The lecture’s box diagram distinguishes content, padding around the content, and margin outside the View. Increasing padding can affect the size needed for a wrap_content View.

Slides: 11, pp. 19–21; 7, p. 68. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Describe why we use device independent pixels
cards.backText:
Android devices have different pixel densities. The same number of physical pixels can occupy different physical sizes on different screens.

Density-independent pixels (dp) make UI sizing scale with density, so a View maintains approximately the same physical size across devices. The slide example shows 32dp = 32px at 160dpi and 32dp = 64px at 320dpi.

Slides: 6, pp. 53–59. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Be able to define a Density-independent Pixel (DP)
cards.backText:
A density-independent pixel (dp / DP) is a virtual sizing unit based on a 160dpi reference screen. At 160dpi, 1dp corresponds to 1 physical pixel.

At higher densities, a dp uses more physical pixels; at lower densities, fewer. It is therefore different from a fixed physical pixel count. Use dp for dimensions such as spacing and View sizes.

Slides: 6, pp. 53–59. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Be able to convert sizes in DPs to actual screen dpi and vice versa
cards.backText:
The review wording says “screen dpi”; a size is converted between dp and pixels (px) using the screen’s density in dots per inch (dpi). A size alone cannot be converted to a density.

From the lecture’s 160dpi reference and 320dpi example:

px = dp × (dpi / 160)
dp = px × (160 / dpi)
  • 32dp at 320dpi: 32 × 320/160 = 64px.
  • 24dp at 240dpi: 24 × 240/160 = 36px.
  • 90px at 240dpi: 90 × 160/240 = 60dp.

The formulas generalize the relationship illustrated in the slides; the lecture diagram does not print these formulas explicitly.

Slides: 6, pp. 58–59. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Define a Scale-independent Pixel (SP)
cards.backText:
A scale-independent pixel (sp / SP) scales like dp and additionally respects the user’s font-size preference. The slides recommend it for text sizing.

android:textSize="18sp"

Remember: dp for general dimensions and spacing; sp for text size so the text follows the user’s font scaling.

Slides: 6, p. 61. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Describe the purpose and basic characteristics of these Android widgets:

  • TextView
  • EditText
  • Button
  • ImageView
  • Spinner
  • CheckBox
  • RadioButton and RadioGroup
  • DatePicker
  • AnalogClock and TextClock
  • VideoView
  • ViewPager
  • ProgressBar
cards.backText:
These are the widgets named in the midterm review:

  • TextView: Displays text such as a label or result; text can be set in XML or changed in Java.
  • EditText: Accepts editable user input; hint prompts the user and inputType configures the expected input.
  • Button: Triggers an action when clicked, commonly through an OnClickListener.
  • ImageView: Displays a drawable image; src chooses it and scaleType controls how it fits.
  • Spinner: Shows the selected item and lets the user choose from a list, supplied through entries or an adapter.
  • CheckBox: An independent checked/unchecked option; multiple CheckBoxes may be checked.
  • RadioButton and RadioGroup: Mutually exclusive choices: selecting one RadioButton in a RadioGroup clears the previous selection.
  • DatePicker: Lets the user select a year, month, and day; supports calendar and spinner presentations.
  • AnalogClock and TextClock: Display the current time with hour/minute hands or formatted text, respectively. TextClock supports 12/24-hour formats and a time zone.
  • VideoView: Displays and plays video; a MediaController supplies playback controls.
  • ViewPager: Presents pages the user moves between by swiping, supplied through an adapter. Supplemental: the slides mention paging but do not explain it in detail.
  • ProgressBar: Indicates work in progress. Indeterminate mode shows ongoing work with an unknown completion amount; determinate mode uses max and progress to show a known amount.

Slides: 7, pp. 7–111; 11, p. 87; 12, p. 75. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

TextView
cards.backText:
TextView displays text, such as a label or result. Its text can be specified in XML or changed from Java.

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/resultText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="@string/app_name"
    android:textSize="20sp" />
TextView result = findViewById(R.id.resultText);
result.setText("Result: 5");
CharSequence displayed = result.getText();

The slides also demonstrate line counts, em-based width, and automatic links. TextView is for displaying text; EditText adds user editing.

Slides: 7, pp. 28–40. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

EditText
cards.backText:
EditText extends TextView to accept and edit user input. It can provide a hint and restrict or configure input through inputType—for example, a number, phone number, email address, or password.

<EditText
    android:id="@+id/nameInput"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:hint="Enter your name"
    android:inputType="textPersonName" />
EditText nameInput = findViewById(R.id.nameInput);
String name = nameInput.getText().toString();

A hint is a prompt shown for empty input; it is different from actual entered text. The inputType examples in the slides configure the kind of input expected.

Slides: 7, pp. 7–18. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

Button
cards.backText:
A Button is a clickable UI control used to trigger an action. It commonly displays a text label and responds through an OnClickListener.

Button submit = findViewById(R.id.submitButton);
submit.setOnClickListener(view -> {
    Toast.makeText(this, "Submitted", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show();
});

The listener is registered during UI setup and executes on a later click. Principal text-related attributes include text, textSize, and textAllCaps.

Slides: 7, pp. 47–52; 6, pp. 41–51. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

ImageView
cards.backText:
ImageView displays an image, usually a drawable resource. Its scaling determines how the image fits inside the View.

<ImageView
    android:layout_width="120dp"
    android:layout_height="120dp"
    android:src="@drawable/logo"
    android:scaleType="fitCenter"
    android:contentDescription="App logo" />

src chooses the image. fitCenter fits it within the available area and centers it while preserving its proportions. The lecture also shows app:srcCompat, padding, contentDescription, and rotation in image examples. This XML assumes a logo drawable exists.

Slides: 7, pp. 68–69; 11, pp. 44, 47–50, 67. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

Spinner
cards.backText:
A Spinner offers a compact selection control: it shows the selected item and lets the user choose from a list of alternatives. The slides demonstrate supplying choices through XML entries and through an adapter.

Spinner choices = findViewById(R.id.versionSpinner);
String selected = choices.getSelectedItem().toString();

android:entries can refer to a string-array resource; android:prompt supplies prompt text. An ArrayAdapter connects a Java array/list of choices to the Spinner’s item Views.

Slides: 7, pp. 41–46; 11, pp. 70–75. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

CheckBox
cards.backText:
A CheckBox represents an independent checked/unchecked choice. Several CheckBoxes can be selected at the same time, so they are useful for options that are not mutually exclusive.

CheckBox option = findViewById(R.id.notificationsCheck);
boolean enabled = option.isChecked();
option.setChecked(true);

Its label comes from text. isChecked() reads its boolean state. Contrast this with RadioButtons in a RadioGroup, where one option is selected.

Slides: 7, pp. 55–57. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

RadioButton and RadioGroup
cards.backText:
A RadioButton represents one choice. A RadioGroup groups RadioButtons so that selecting one clears the previously selected option: the choices are mutually exclusive.

Clicking an already selected RadioButton leaves it checked. The slides show a RadioGroup listener reporting the checked ID and clearCheck() clearing the selection.

RadioGroup group = findViewById(R.id.answerGroup);
group.setOnCheckedChangeListener((radioGroup, checkedId) -> {
    if (checkedId == R.id.optionA) {
        resultText.setText("A selected");
    }
});
// Clear all RadioButton selections in the group:
group.clearCheck();

Slides: 7, pp. 63–67. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

DatePicker
cards.backText:
A DatePicker lets the user select a date—year, month, and day. The slides show calendar and spinner presentations, configured through datePickerMode.

DatePicker picker = findViewById(R.id.datePicker);
picker.init(2026, 9, 8, (view, year, month, day) -> {
    // Android month values are zero-based; 9 means October.
    dateText.setText(day + "/" + (month + 1) + "/" + year);
});

init supplies the starting date and an OnDateChangedListener. The callback receives the newly selected values. This is an adaptation of the lecture’s init/listener example.

Slides: 7, pp. 70–73. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

AnalogClock and TextClock
cards.backText:
• AnalogClock: the lecture’s clock widget displays the current time with hour and minute hands. The slides describe minute updates and no second hand.
  • TextClock: displays the current time as formatted text. It supports format12Hour, format24Hour, and timeZone attributes.
<TextClock
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:format12Hour="h:mm a"
    android:format24Hour="HH:mm" />

These descriptions follow the professor’s widget material. They display time, unlike DatePicker, which lets the user select a date.

Slides: 7, pp. 101–105. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

VideoView
cards.backText:
VideoView displays and plays video. The slides attach a MediaController so users can control playback and set a video URI before starting.

VideoView video = findViewById(R.id.videoView);
MediaController controls = new MediaController(this);
controls.setAnchorView(video);
video.setMediaController(controls);
video.setVideoURI(Uri.parse("https://example.com/video.mp4"));
video.start();

The URI here is a placeholder: use a real video source. The lecture’s network-video example also requires <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" /> in the manifest.

Slides: 7, pp. 106–111. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

ViewPager
cards.backText:
The slides list ViewPager / ViewPager2 among UI tools and mention paging fragments, but do not explain it in detail.

Supplemental explanation: A ViewPager presents a sequence of pages that the user moves between by swiping. Pages can be Views or fragment-based screens supplied through an adapter. It is useful for sibling pages, and it can be paired with tabs to indicate or select the current page. Focus on its paging/swiping role; no detailed implementation is supplied in the lectures.

Slides: 11, p. 87; 12, p. 75. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Purpose and basic characteristics

ProgressBar
cards.backText:
A ProgressBar communicates that work is happening or how much has completed.

  • Indeterminate: indicates ongoing work when the completion amount is unknown; the slides show circular indicators in several sizes.
  • Determinate: shows a known completion amount, typically using a horizontal bar. max sets the range, progress sets the completed amount, and secondaryProgress can show a second amount.
ProgressBar bar = findViewById(R.id.progressBar);
bar.setMax(100);
bar.setProgress(75);

With max=100 and progress=75, the bar represents 75% completion. The horizontal style shown in XML is style="?android:attr/progressBarStyleHorizontal".

Slides: 7, pp. 76–89. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

For TextView, EditView, Button, and ImageView be able to name a few principal XML attributes and provide their meaning (i.e., attributes other than common ones, such as layout_width)
cards.backText:
“EditView” is interpreted as EditText, matching the review’s widget list. Know attributes beyond the common width/height properties:

  • TextView: text = displayed text or @string resource; textSize = text size (sp); lines/minLines/maxLines = line count constraints; ems/minEms/maxEms = width in text-based em units; autoLink = automatic link handling for matching text.
  • EditText: hint = empty-field prompt; inputType = expected input/keyboard type (for example number or textEmailAddress); lines = number of displayed lines; it also inherits TextView properties.
  • Button: text = label; textAllCaps = whether the label is shown in uppercase; textSize = label size.
  • ImageView: src or app:srcCompat = drawable image; scaleType = image scaling/alignment; contentDescription = descriptive text for the image; rotation = angle of rotation.
<EditText
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:hint="Email address"
    android:inputType="textEmailAddress" />

Slides: 7, pp. 9–14, 29–39, 50–51, 68–69; 6, pp. 41–44; 11, pp. 47–50. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Describe the purpose of the R.java class and the findViewById method
cards.backText:
findViewById retrieves a View with a specified resource ID from the loaded View hierarchy. It gives Java code access to the object so you can read/change properties and register listeners.

setContentView(R.layout.activity_main);
TextView label = findViewById(R.id.messageText);
label.setText("Hello");

The slides repeatedly use R.layout for layouts and R.id for View identifiers.

Supplemental explanation: R / R.java is the build-generated resource class. Its nested groups identify resources such as R.layout.activity_main, R.id.messageText, and R.string.app_name. Use these identifiers to refer to resources from Java; do not manually edit the generated class. This role is not directly explained in the supplied slides.

Slides: 6, pp. 17–18, 46–51; 7, p. 6; 11, pp. 6, 74. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
5. Views and Widgets

Describe how a View’s properties can be accessed and modified programmatically
cards.backText:
After inflating/loading the layout, retrieve a View by its ID, then use its getters, setters, and listener-registration methods. XML gives initial properties; Java can access or modify them while the app runs.

setContentView(R.layout.activity_main);
EditText name = findViewById(R.id.nameInput);
TextView greeting = findViewById(R.id.greetingText);
Button button = findViewById(R.id.greetButton);

button.setOnClickListener(view -> {
    String entered = name.getText().toString();
    greeting.setText("Hello, " + entered);
});

Other slide examples include CheckBox.isChecked(), ProgressBar.setProgress(), Spinner.getSelectedItem(), and RadioGroup.clearCheck(). The referenced View IDs must exist in the loaded layout.

Slides: 6, pp. 46–51; 7, pp. 11, 31, 46, 57, 66–67, 83. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Carefully review chapter 8 and lecture slides on eLC
cards.backText:
Use Lecture 11: IntroductionToLayouts for this section. Focus on LinearLayout pp. 24–38 and ConstraintLayout pp. 88–119; also review FrameLayout pp. 45–51, TableLayout pp. 52–56, sizes/margins/padding pp. 16–21, and adapters pp. 70–75.

Lecture 6, pp. 33–44, gives a nested LinearLayout example. Practice translating arrangements into XML rather than only recognizing names.

Slides: 11, pp. 3–119; 6, pp. 33–44. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Describe what is a layout in Android
cards.backText:
A layout is a container that determines how its child Views are arranged and sized. Different layout classes apply different placement rules—for example, a row/column, stacked Views, table cells, or constraints.

The layout itself is a View, typically a ViewGroup. It can contain widgets and other layouts. The UI hierarchy can be declared in XML or created in Java.

Slides: 6, pp. 19–22; 11, pp. 3–4, 9–15. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Explain the difference between layouts specified in XML and programmatically
cards.backText:
XML layout: declare the View hierarchy and initial properties in a resource file. Android inflates it into View objects, for example through setContentView(R.layout.activity_main).

Programmatic layout: construct View objects in Java, set their properties, add them to a ViewGroup, and use the result as the Activity’s content. Both approaches produce a View hierarchy.

LinearLayout layout = new LinearLayout(this);
layout.setOrientation(LinearLayout.VERTICAL);
TextView label = new TextView(this);
label.setText("Hello");
layout.addView(label, new LinearLayout.LayoutParams(
    LinearLayout.LayoutParams.WRAP_CONTENT,
    LinearLayout.LayoutParams.WRAP_CONTENT));
setContentView(layout);

This fragment goes inside an Activity. XML keeps a static arrangement in resources; Java explicitly constructs and can change the hierarchy while running.

Slides: 11, pp. 5–8. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Describe the main principles governing placement of Views in LinearLayout, FrameLayout, TableLayout, and ConstraintLayout.
cards.backText:
• LinearLayout: places children sequentially in one horizontal row or vertical column.
  • FrameLayout: places children in a shared area, potentially overlapping/stacked.
  • TableLayout: organizes children into rows and columns using TableRows.
  • ConstraintLayout: positions/sizes children using relationships to the parent and other Views.

Slides: 11, pp. 24–56, 88–119. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

View placement principles

LinearLayout (you should know it well)
cards.backText:
LinearLayout arranges children in XML order along one axis: orientation="horizontal" gives a row; orientation="vertical" gives a column.

  • gravity: positions the contents/children within the layout’s available space.
  • layout_gravity: a child’s requested alignment within its parent, where applicable.
  • layout_weight: distributes remaining space among children in proportion to their weights. For equal widths in a row, use width=0dp and equal weights; for a column, use height=0dp along the weighted axis.
<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:orientation="horizontal"
    android:padding="16dp">
    <Button android:id="@+id/leftButton"
        android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_weight="1" android:text="Left" />
    <Button android:id="@+id/rightButton"
        android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_weight="1" android:text="Right" />
</LinearLayout>

The two buttons share the row’s available width equally. Here 0dp works with LinearLayout weight; it is not ConstraintLayout match-constraint sizing.

Slides: 11, pp. 24–38. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

View placement principles

FrameLayout
cards.backText:
FrameLayout places children within the same rectangular area. They can overlap; later children are drawn on top of earlier children. The default placement is at the top-left, and layout_gravity can position a child elsewhere.

<FrameLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="200dp">
    <ImageView android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent" android:src="@drawable/photo"
        android:contentDescription="Photo" />
    <TextView android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:text="Caption"
        android:layout_gravity="bottom|center_horizontal" />
</FrameLayout>

The caption overlays the photo. The slide attribute table also lists foreground, foregroundGravity, and measureAllChildren. The sample assumes the photo drawable exists.

Slides: 11, pp. 45–51. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

View placement principles

TableLayout
cards.backText:
TableLayout organizes content into rows and columns. A TableRow contains the Views for one row. A column’s width is determined by its widest cell, and the number of columns depends on the row with the most columns.

  • layout_column: places a child in a specified zero-based column, allowing gaps.
  • layout_span: makes a child occupy multiple columns.
  • stretchColumns: lets chosen columns take extra space; * chooses all columns.
  • shrinkColumns: lets chosen columns shrink.
  • collapseColumns: hides chosen columns.
<TableLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:stretchColumns="*">
    <TableRow android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content">
        <Button android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:text="Left" />
        <Button android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:text="Right" />
    </TableRow>
    <TableRow android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content">
        <Button android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:layout_column="1"
            android:text="Below right" />
    </TableRow>
</TableLayout>

The second row’s button is in column 1, below the right-hand button in row 1.

Slides: 11, pp. 52–56. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

View placement principles

ConstraintLayout (you should know it well)
cards.backText:
ConstraintLayout places Views by relationships to the parent or other Views. Each child needs enough constraints to determine its horizontal and vertical position. Sizing can be fixed, wrap_content, or match constraints (0dp).

  • Edges: start/end/top/bottom constraints align to the corresponding edge of another View or parent; a top-to-bottom relation places one View below another.
  • Bias: controls placement between opposing constraints when the View has remaining space; 0.5 is centered.
  • Margins: add space at constrained edges.
  • Chains: link Views across an axis; slide examples include spread, spread_inside, packed, and weighted chains.
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent">
    <TextView android:id="@+id/titleText"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Title" android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent" />
    <Button android:id="@+id/continueButton"
        android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Continue" android:layout_margin="16dp"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toBottomOf="@id/titleText"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent" />
</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

The title is horizontally centered at the top. The button sits below it and fills the width between its start/end constraints, with 16dp margins. Unlike the title’s wrap_content width, the button’s 0dp width expands to satisfy its opposing constraints.

Slides: 11, pp. 88–119; 10, pp. 47–48. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

For Linear and Constraint layouts, be able to create an actual XML layout, given a picture of a desired arrangement and sizing of views
cards.backText:
Translate the desired arrangement into parent type, ordering/relationships, sizes, and spacing. Include namespace declarations and the width/height of each View.

Example target A: two equal-width buttons in one row, with 16dp padding. Use a horizontal LinearLayout and give each button width=0dp, weight=1:

<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:orientation="horizontal"
    android:padding="16dp">
    <Button android:id="@+id/leftButton"
        android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_weight="1" android:text="Left" />
    <Button android:id="@+id/rightButton"
        android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_weight="1" android:text="Right" />
</LinearLayout>

Example target B: a title centered near the top, with a full-width button below it and 16dp margins. Use top/start/end constraints; the button’s width=0dp matches its start/end constraints:

<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent">
    <TextView android:id="@+id/titleText"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Title" android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent" />
    <Button android:id="@+id/continueButton"
        android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Continue" android:layout_margin="16dp"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toBottomOf="@id/titleText"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent" />
</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

These are practice arrangements built from the rules in the slide examples. Be able to explain why each orientation, weight, constraint, and size value produces the arrangement.

Slides: 6, pp. 33–44; 11, pp. 27–38, 93–107, 114–119. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

XML practice — Easy LinearLayout

Write XML for the picture using one vertical LinearLayout.

  • Root fills the parent and has 16dp padding on every side.
  • Welcome is a TextView with wrap_content width/height and 20sp text.
  • Continue is a Button with match_parent width and wrap_content height, 16dp below the label.

The picture is schematic; use the stated sizes and gaps. Match the arrangement, not theme-specific styling.
cards.backText:
One valid XML solution

<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical"
    android:padding="16dp">

    <TextView
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Welcome"
        android:textSize="20sp" />

    <Button
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        android:text="Continue" />
</LinearLayout>

Why this works

  • orientation="vertical" stacks the two child Views in XML order.
  • Root padding keeps both children inset from its edges. The button's marginTop supplies the gap.
  • match_parent fills the available padded width; wrap_content fits the contents.

Use this as a layout resource and display it with setContentView(R.layout.activity_main); in your Activity. For ConstraintLayout, the project needs the ConstraintLayout library used in class. Equivalent XML that satisfies the requirements is also valid.

Original practice exercise and generated diagram based on the professor's layout material, not an actual exam question. Slides: 11, pp. 15–21, 24–28.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

XML practice — Semi-difficult LinearLayout

Write XML for the picture using nested LinearLayouts.

  • Root fills the parent, is vertical, and has 16dp padding.
  • Choose an action is a wrap_content TextView with 20sp text.
  • A full-width horizontal row sits 16dp below the label; Yes and No have equal widths and a 12dp gap.
  • Close is a full-width Button 16dp below the row. All button heights are wrap_content.

The picture is schematic; use the stated sizes and gaps. Match the arrangement, not theme-specific styling.
cards.backText:
One valid XML solution

<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical"
    android:padding="16dp">

    <TextView
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Choose an action"
        android:textSize="20sp" />

    <LinearLayout
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        android:orientation="horizontal">

        <Button
            android:layout_width="0dp"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:layout_weight="1"
            android:layout_marginEnd="12dp"
            android:text="Yes" />

        <Button
            android:layout_width="0dp"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:layout_weight="1"
            android:text="No" />
    </LinearLayout>

    <Button
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        android:text="Close" />
</LinearLayout>

Why this works

  • The outer vertical layout stacks the label, button row, and Close button.
  • The inner horizontal layout puts Yes and No side by side.
  • width="0dp" with equal layout_weight="1" shares the space remaining after the 12dp margin equally.
  • Only Yes has marginEnd="12dp", so the gap is 12dp, not 24dp.

Use this as a layout resource and display it with setContentView(R.layout.activity_main); in your Activity. For ConstraintLayout, the project needs the ConstraintLayout library used in class. Equivalent XML that satisfies the requirements is also valid.

Original practice exercise and generated diagram based on the professor's layout material, not an actual exam question. Slides: 11, pp. 24–38.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

XML practice — Easy ConstraintLayout

Write XML for the picture using one ConstraintLayout.

  • Root fills the parent. Both Buttons use wrap_content width and height.
  • Save is 16dp from the parent's start edge and 16dp from its top.
  • Cancel starts 16dp after Save's end edge. Their top edges align.
  • Use IDs saveButton and cancelButton.

The picture is schematic; use the stated sizes and gaps. Match the arrangement, not theme-specific styling.
cards.backText:
One valid XML solution

<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent">

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/saveButton"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginStart="16dp"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        android:text="Save"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent" />

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/cancelButton"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginStart="16dp"
        android:text="Cancel"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toEndOf="@id/saveButton"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="@id/saveButton" />
</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

Why this works

  • Save has a horizontal start-to-parent constraint and a vertical top-to-parent constraint.
  • Cancel uses Start_toEndOf Save plus a 16dp start margin.
  • Cancel's Top_toTopOf Save aligns their top edges; it does not need another top margin.
  • Each View has at least one horizontal and one vertical constraint.

Use this as a layout resource and display it with setContentView(R.layout.activity_main); in your Activity. For ConstraintLayout, the project needs the ConstraintLayout library used in class. Equivalent XML that satisfies the requirements is also valid.

Original practice exercise and generated diagram based on the professor's layout material, not an actual exam question. Slides: 11, pp. 93–101.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

XML practice — Semi-difficult ConstraintLayout

Write XML for the picture using one ConstraintLayout, with no nested layout.

  • Root fills the parent.
  • Profile is a 20sp wrap_content TextView, centered horizontally, 16dp below the parent top.
  • Your name is the hint of an EditText: stretch it between 16dp start/end margins, 24dp below the title. Height is wrap_content.
  • Save uses wrap_content width/height, sits 16dp below the input, and ends 16dp from the parent end.
  • Use IDs titleText, nameInput, and saveButton.

The picture is schematic; use the stated sizes and gaps. Match the arrangement, not theme-specific styling.
cards.backText:
One valid XML solution

<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent">

    <TextView
        android:id="@+id/titleText"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        android:text="Profile"
        android:textSize="20sp"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent" />

    <EditText
        android:id="@+id/nameInput"
        android:layout_width="0dp"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginStart="16dp"
        android:layout_marginEnd="16dp"
        android:layout_marginTop="24dp"
        android:hint="Your name"
        android:inputType="textPersonName"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toBottomOf="@id/titleText" />

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/saveButton"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_marginEnd="16dp"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
        android:text="Save"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toBottomOf="@id/nameInput" />
</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

Why this works

  • The wrap_content title is centered by constraining both its start and end to the parent.
  • The input's width="0dp" means match constraints: fill between its start/end constraints after margins.
  • Top_toBottomOf places the input below the title and Save below the input.
  • Save has an end constraint and a top constraint, so its position is fully specified.

Use this as a layout resource and display it with setContentView(R.layout.activity_main); in your Activity. For ConstraintLayout, the project needs the ConstraintLayout library used in class. Equivalent XML that satisfies the requirements is also valid.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

For LinearLayout, FrameLayout, TableLayout, and ConstraintLayout, name the principal XML attributes and explain their meanings.
cards.backText:
• LinearLayout: orientation (row/column), gravity (alignment of contents), child layout_gravity (child alignment), layout_weight (share of remaining space), weightSum (specified total weight).
  • FrameLayout: child layout_gravity (placement), foreground (drawable overlay), foregroundGravity (foreground alignment), measureAllChildren (whether all children are measured, including gone children).
  • TableLayout: stretchColumns, shrinkColumns, collapseColumns (column behavior); child layout_column (zero-based column) and layout_span (number of columns).
  • ConstraintLayout: layout_constraintStart_toStartOf / End_toEndOf / Top_toTopOf / Top_toBottomOf (edge relationships), layout_constraintHorizontal_bias / Vertical_bias (placement between opposing constraints), layout_constraintHorizontal_chainStyle (chain distribution). Constraint attributes use the app prefix.

Dimensions and margins are child layout parameters as well. Match the attribute to the layout class: layout_weight belongs to LinearLayout; constraint relationships belong to ConstraintLayout.

Slides: 11, pp. 25–38, 46–55, 93–119. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Describe the basic difference between match_parent, wrap_content, and match_constraint (0dp) when specifying View’s width and height.
cards.backText:
• match_parent: occupy the parent’s available size along that dimension, accounting for the parent’s padding and layout spacing.
  • wrap_content: use the size needed for the View’s content and its padding.
  • match_constraint (0dp in ConstraintLayout): let constraints determine the size. With opposing start/end constraints and width=0dp, the View fills the space between those constraints, accounting for margins.

Context matters: 0dp in a weighted LinearLayout means the base size is zero and weight supplies its allocated space. It is not automatically match_constraint in every layout.

android:layout_width="0dp"
app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"

Slides: 11, pp. 17–19, 27–38, 104–107. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Describe the purpose of View margins when defining a layout.
cards.backText:
Margins provide space outside a View’s bounds, separating it from neighboring Views or the parent’s boundaries. Padding provides space inside the View, around its content.

android:layout_margin="16dp"
android:layout_marginStart="8dp"
android:layout_marginTop="12dp"

You can specify all sides or individual sides. In ConstraintLayout, a margin at a constrained edge sets spacing between that edge and the edge it is constrained to.

Slides: 11, pp. 16–21, 93–107. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Explain what is an ArrayAdapter and why is it needed
cards.backText:
An ArrayAdapter connects an array/list of data items to the item Views displayed by a list-style widget, such as a Spinner or ListView. It uses an item layout to render each data item.

String[] versions = { "Android 15", "Android 16", "Android 17" };
ArrayAdapter<String> adapter = new ArrayAdapter<>(
    this, android.R.layout.simple_spinner_item, versions);
adapter.setDropDownViewResource(
    android.R.layout.simple_spinner_dropdown_item);
Spinner spinner = findViewById(R.id.versionSpinner);
spinner.setAdapter(adapter);

The data array supplies the items; the layout resource supplies their appearance; setAdapter attaches the bridge to the widget. Inside a Fragment, use the appropriate host context, as in the fragment examples.

Slides: 11, pp. 70–75, 78–79; 7, pp. 23–27, 41–46. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Explain when nesting of layouts is useful/necessary
cards.backText:
Nesting layouts is useful when different parts of a screen need different placement rules. For example, a vertical LinearLayout can hold a heading, then a horizontal LinearLayout containing two buttons, then another result View.

The slides’ counter app uses this kind of nesting, and later examples combine other layouts. A nested layout is itself a child ViewGroup. The lecture also warns that excessive nesting can be suboptimal, so use it where the arrangement benefits from separate containers.

Slides: 6, pp. 33–44; 11, pp. 22–23, 38, 63–64. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Is layout itself a View? What is the basic superclass of most of the layout classes?
cards.backText:
Yes. A layout is a View. Most layout classes have ViewGroup as their base superclass, and ViewGroup extends View.

ViewGroup is a special View that contains and manages child Views. Consequently, a layout can itself be a child of another layout, producing a hierarchy.

Slides: 6, p. 19; 11, pp. 9, 15, 63. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Be able to provide a (small) set of attributes and their values to achieve a given layout of Views when using Linear, Table, and Constraint layout
cards.backText:
Linear target: two equal-width buttons in a horizontal row. Set parent orientation="horizontal"; set each child layout_width="0dp" and layout_weight="1"; use wrap_content heights.

Table target: put a button in the second column of a row. Place it inside a TableRow and set layout_column="1". To span two columns, set layout_span="2". Parent stretchColumns="*" allows all columns to stretch.

Constraint target: put B below A, aligned to the parent’s start, with a 16dp vertical gap:

android:layout_width="wrap_content"
android:layout_height="wrap_content"
android:layout_marginTop="16dp"
app:layout_constraintTop_toBottomOf="@id/viewA"
app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"

For B to fill the width, switch width to 0dp and add End_toEndOf="parent". These attributes belong on B; viewA must have the referenced ID and its own constraints.

Slides: 11, pp. 25–38, 54–55, 93–119. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

7. Fragments

Carefully review chapter 9 and lecture slides on eLC

Focus on how a selected list index is saved/restored and how the same details fragment can be used in different Activity arrangements.

Slides: 12, pp. 3–69; 11, pp. 82–86. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
7. Fragments

Describe why fragments are useful
cards.backText:
Fragments divide an Activity’s UI and behavior into modular pieces. Each can have its own layout and lifecycle, while being hosted by an Activity.

They are useful for adapting to different screen sizes/orientations. In a narrow/portrait arrangement, a list and details can appear separately; in a wide/landscape arrangement, the same pieces can appear side by side in one Activity. The lecture examples show this reuse without duplicating the list/details implementation.

Slides: 12, pp. 3–10, 24–39, 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
7. Fragments

Explain how fragments promote code reuse
cards.backText:
Put the layout and behavior for one UI feature into a Fragment class, then host that class wherever it is needed. Different Activities or layouts can reuse the same fragment instead of copying its UI and logic.

The lecture’s master/detail examples reuse list and details fragments: the portrait arrangement uses separate screens, while the landscape arrangement places both pieces together. The reusable unit is the fragment’s implementation; the host controls how it is presented.

Slides: 12, pp. 3–10, 24–39, 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
7. Fragments

Describe the relationship between Activities and Fragments
cards.backText:
An Activity hosts Fragments. The Activity provides the screen/window and manages its fragments through a FragmentManager. A Fragment provides a portion of the UI/behavior and has its own lifecycle coordinated with its host.

  • One Activity can host several Fragments.
  • A Fragment can be reused in different Activity/layout arrangements.
  • The Fragment creates its own View hierarchy in onCreateView; that View hierarchy has a lifetime distinct from the Fragment object.
  • FragmentTransactions add, remove, or replace fragments in the host’s containers.
FragmentManager manager = getSupportFragmentManager();

Slides: 12, pp. 3–23. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
7. Fragments

Describe the fragment life cycle – name and describe the main fragment callbacks
cards.backText:
Know the lifecycle callbacks named by the androidx fragment lecture:

  • onAttach: attached to the host/context.
  • onCreate: initialize the Fragment itself.
  • onCreateView: create/inflate and return the Fragment’s View hierarchy.
  • onViewCreated: set up the created Views and their listeners; the lecture points to this instead of the deprecated onActivityCreated.
  • onStart: Fragment becomes visible.
  • onResume: active/resumed for interaction.
  • onPause: leaving the resumed state.
  • onStop: no longer started/visible.
  • onDestroyView: the Fragment’s View hierarchy is destroyed.
  • onDestroy: Fragment instance is being destroyed.
  • onDetach: detached from the host.

Creation order: attach → create → createView → viewCreated → start → resume. Normal teardown passes through pause → stop → destroyView → destroy → detach. The View hierarchy can be destroyed while the Fragment instance is retained on the fragment back stack, so distinguish onDestroyView from onDestroy.

@Override
public View onCreateView(LayoutInflater inflater,
                         ViewGroup container, Bundle savedInstanceState) {
    return inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_details, container, false);
}

Slides: 12, pp. 11–12, 22–23, 46–64. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
7. Fragments

Explain the need for FragmentTransactions
cards.backText:
A FragmentTransaction groups changes to fragments managed by a FragmentManager. Use it to add, replace, remove, show, or hide fragments, then commit the changes.

FragmentManager manager = getSupportFragmentManager();
FragmentTransaction transaction = manager.beginTransaction();
transaction.replace(R.id.detailsContainer, new DetailsFragment());
transaction.addToBackStack(null);
transaction.commit();

The container must exist in the Activity’s layout. addToBackStack makes this change reversible through the fragment back stack; it is optional when that navigation behavior is not wanted. commit() submits the changes; creating a transaction alone does not display the replacement.

Slides: 12, pp. 13–20, 54, 68. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
7. Fragments

Describe the difference between ListView and ListFragment
cards.backText:
ListView is a View/widget that displays a scrolling list. It needs an adapter to supply its rows.

ListFragment is a specialized Fragment that provides a list-based UI around a ListView. It has a Fragment lifecycle and offers convenience methods such as setListAdapter and getListView, plus the onListItemClick callback.

@Override
public void onListItemClick(ListView list, View view,
                            int position, long id) {
    showDetails(position);
}

This method goes in a ListFragment subclass; showDetails is an application-defined helper. A custom ListFragment layout uses the expected @android:id/list identifier for its ListView. The widget and the Fragment hosting it are different types of objects.

Slides: 11, pp. 82–86; 12, pp. 40, 52–56. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

8. Navigational patterns

Carefully review chapter 10 and lecture slides on eLC

The supplied slides cover Up/parent Activity declarations in Lecture 8, pp. 65–69 and master/detail fragment arrangements in Lecture 12, pp. 24–39 and 65–69. No dedicated navigation lecture is present in the supplied folder.

The cards for the remaining navigation patterns explicitly label explanations added to fill those gaps. They cover only the navigation bullets requested in the review; no textbook material has been added.
